extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, War Department administrators, post and company commanders, judge advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing types, grounds, procedures, and effects of Army discharges (honorable, without honor, dishonorable, by purchase, by favor, disability, etc.), with case-based guidance and procedural requirements. Intended as operational/legal guidance for officials handling separations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — requirement of opportunity to defend
rubrics_metrics.description: To discharge him summarily without honor, without giving him an opportunity to present a defense, would appear to work an injustice and to establish a dangerous precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commanding general should not summarily discharge a soldier 'without honor' for misconduct unless the soldier has been given an opportunity to make a defense; summary discharges without permitting defense are generally improper (citing C. 22272, Oct. 25, 1907; June 7, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — serious offenses should be tried, not summarily discharged
rubrics_metrics.description: Soldiers charged with crimes (e.g., sodomy) should not be discharged without honor but should be tried by a competent court by whom the facts should be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allegations are criminal in nature, justice requires trial by competent court rather than summary discharge; applicable to sensitive or serious accusations (C. 19547, Apr. 19, 1906; 19539, Apr. 18, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — not to be used where guilt is doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: It would not be proper to discharge without honor unless there were no doubt of his guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations for DWOH (discharge without honor) for misconduct (e.g., indecent proposals) should be withheld where doubt remains; command action should not substitute for clear adjudication (C. 20615, Feb. 2, 1909; Aug. 27, 1909; 24004, Sept. 2, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — effect of prior trial/acquittal or punishment less than discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: If a soldier was tried and acquitted, or tried and given punishment less than discharge, a discharge without honor primarily on account of said alleged offenses would not be proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior court-martial acquittals or lesser punishments for the same alleged offenses generally preclude subsequently giving a discharge without honor for those same allegations (C. 10584, Feb. 1895; 21901, Jan. 21, 1909; G. 1512, July 2, 1895; 15533, Nov. 24, 1903; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — exception where conviction set aside for procedural defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Although improper to discharge a soldier without honor on account of charges for which he has been tried and convicted, the discharge without honor may be used in the case of a soldier who has been convicted and the reviewing authority, acting not on the merits but because of defects in procedure, sets aside or mitigates the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If convictions are set aside or mitigated for procedural/record defects (not on merits), DWOH may still be imposed as the effective corrective/separative measure (C. 25915, Dec. 10, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances allowing discharge without trial (enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) When a soldier is discharged without trial on account of fraudulent enlistment; (b) when he is discharged without trial on account of having been disqualified for service, physically or in character, through his own fault; (c) when the discharge is on account of imprisonment under sentence of a civil court; (d) when at the time of the soldier's discharge, at or after the expiration of his term of enlistment, he is in confinement under the sentence of a general court-martial which does not provide for dishonorable discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories set out when a soldier may be separated without trial yet be classified 'without honor' — used as legal bases for non-trial separations in specified situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds/examples for discharge without honor (illustrative list)
rubrics_metrics.description: An established case of desertion; being in a penitentiary under civil sentence at enlistment expiration; worthlessness; sentenced to a workhouse; expressing sympathy with enemy; disease contracted through misconduct before enlistment; refusal of vaccination; convictions for burglary, theft, homicide (even if pardoned), inefficiency; being unfit associate; sentencing to imprisonment by civil courts; alcoholic dementia; unfaithful service; obscene/insulting letters; being in hands of civil authorities at enlistment expiration; seduction admitting guilt; indecent exposure; incorrigibility and drinking; introducing narcotics into prison; moral incapacity; totally unfit to have been enlisted; attempt at suicide; insanity at time of enlistment; defects in court record; etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion enumerates many concrete examples and case citations where DWOH has been held appropriate. These serve as precedent-based illustrations, not an exclusive closed list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — effect when sentence later approved or disapproved
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval by a department commander of a previously disapproved dishonorable discharge may result in separation under circumstances not honorable but treated as 'discharge without honor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a department commander first disapproves and later approves a sentence leading to separation, the discharge may be treated as without honor rather than formally 'dishonorable' depending on procedural posture (C. 11609, Nov. 8, 1901).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge — definition and prerequisite (court-martial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dishonorable discharge is a discharge given pursuant to the sentence of a general court-martial when specifically awarded by or necessarily involved in such sentence; being a punishment, it can only be authorized by sentence of a court-martial after trial and conviction, and no executive or military official (except in executing such a sentence) can legally give or order such discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dishonorable discharge is strictly a punitive outcome of general court-martial conviction; it cannot be lawfully imposed administratively (P. 142, 267, Aug., 1890; a. 5870, Feb. 21, 1899; 7102, Oct. 5, 1899).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge — imprisonment in penitentiary involves dishonorable status
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier is sentenced by court-martial to imprisonment in a penitentiary and the sentence does not also direct dishonorable discharge, it nevertheless involves such discharge, for the dishonorable status of confinement in a penitentiary is incompatible with the honorable status of a soldier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A penitentiary sentence imposed by court-martial is treated as carrying dishonorable separation consequences even if the sentence text omits explicit discharge (C. 1226, Apr. 25, 1895; 12623, May 15, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge — civil employment and collateral effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A dishonorable discharge entails per se no disqualification for civil employment under the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past opinions have held D.D. by itself does not automatically bar federal civil employment (R. 8, 91, Mar., 1864; 28, 250, Nov., 1868; 31, 296, Apr., 1871; 34, 623, Nov., 1873).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge — rescission of enlistment and loss of contingent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier is dishonorably discharged from the military service in the operation of a sentence of court-martial, the operation of such discharge is to rescind the soldier's contract of enlistment, and in the operation of such rescission all contingent rights and benefits, present and future, which are conditioned upon honest and faithful service on the part of the soldier fall with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D.D. nullifies the contractual basis for benefits contingent on honest and faithful service (C. 27073, July 22, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability discharge on surgeon's certificate — honorable when duty-related
rubrics_metrics.description: If during his term of enlistment a soldier becomes incapable of rendering service on account of disability contracted in the line of duty, he is granted a discharge on a surgeon's certificate of disability; such discharge is honorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disability incurred in line of duty warrants honorable discharge on medical certificate (C. 20754, Nov. 23, 1906; Mar. 30, 1908). Where disability existed at enlistment but not due to soldier's fault, discharge should be honorable (C. 3540, Sept. 22, 1897).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge by way of favor — generally illegal; limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discharges by way of favor as distinguished from purchase are illegal and will not be granted except in case of dependent parent after one year's service of the soldier; a soldier shall not be discharged by way of favor until he shall have served one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor discharges are tightly restricted; Secretary of War discretion and statutory exceptions apply; some long-service cases may justify favor discharge depending on character of service (C. 15717, Dec. 28, 1911; C. 12607, May 14, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge by purchase (act of June 16, 1890) — authority and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 of the act of June 16, 1890 authorizes the President, in time of peace, in his discretion and under such rules and upon such conditions as he shall prescribe, to permit any enlisted man to purchase his discharge from the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President may permit purchase even if prior service not honest and faithful; Army Regulations prescribe rules/conditions; purchase eligibility may require minimum service (periods absent without leave excluded), purchases may be forbidden in certain territories (e.g., outside continental U.S.), previous Marine Corps service may not count toward Army service, Philippine Scouts are included under the act (C. 1340, May 10, 1895; C. 7617, Jan. 27, 1900; C. 22731, Feb. 10, 1908; C. 18391, Aug. 7, 1905; C. 18157, June 14, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge by purchase — honorable character and immigration effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A discharge by purchase is an honorable discharge within the meaning of section 2106, R. S., which waives declaration of intention to become a citizen in case of an honorably discharged soldier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchase discharges are treated as honorable for execution matters, statements of character, and statutory benefits (C. 22923, Mar. 19, 1908; C. 27037, July 15, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for determining 'honest and faithful' service at term expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations provide that when a company commander deems the service of an enlisted man not honest and faithful, he shall, if practicable, so notify the soldier at least 30 days prior to discharge and shall at the same time notify the commanding officer, who will in every such case convene a board of officers, three, if practicable, to determine whether the soldier's service has been honest and faithful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notice/board requirement applies to discharges at expiration of term of enlistment; however, it is directory only and does not restrict the Secretary of War's authority under the fourth article of war to annul enlistment contracts in the public interest (C. 20754, Nov. 23, 1906; 23259, Apr. 9, 1909; C. 5943, March, 1899; 12942, July 11, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: General Orders No. 40 (Spanish War enlistments) — discharge at close of war, timing and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: General Orders 40 provided that men enlisted or reenlisted during the war may be informed they will be granted their discharges at the close of the war upon their individual applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such discharges must be claimed within a reasonable time after war's close; soldiers under charges, awaiting trials, or serving sentences are not entitled to discharge under this order; waiver attempts are ineffective; the provision empowers Executive selection and does not create individual enforceable rights before the applicable time (C. 6569, June, 1899; C. 6731, July 22, 1899; C. 5787, Feb. 3, 1899).

rubrics_metrics.name: State court habeas corpus discharge orders — invalid as discharge; Secretary issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a State court on habeas corpus proceedings ordered that a soldier in the military service of the United States be discharged therefrom, the court was without jurisdiction in the matter and its order was absolutely void and without effect as a discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a soldier is released by civil courts on habeas corpus, the Secretary of War should cause a discharge certificate to be issued where appropriate; however state-court orders attempting to discharge are void (C. 2739, Nov. 17, 1896; P. 32, 313-319, May, 1889; C. 394, Sept., 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Company or unit refusal to obey orders — collective discharge without honor
rubrics_metrics.description: A company of volunteers that refused to proceed to a certain point when ordered to go there, was subsequently duly mustered out because of its refusal to obey the order; members of the company were discharged without honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective refusal to obey lawful orders may justify unit mustering out and DWOH for members (C. 1915, Dec. 1895).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers — summary dismissals and discharges without honor for unfitness/fraud/AWOL
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteer officer summarily dismissed on account of unfitness caused by his own fault is discharged without honor; similarly where officer was summarily 'dropped' for absence without leave; fraud in mustering-in may warrant dismissal without honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary dismissals of officers for unfitness, contemptuous conduct, quitting guard, or fraud are treated as discharges without honor (P. 62, 403, Mar. 1892; P. 46, 389, Apr. 1891; C. 1789, Oct. 18, 1896; C. 9335, Nov. 26, 1900; C. 16822, Sept. 2, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character notation on discharge — refers to soldier and man
rubrics_metrics.description: The notation as to character entered upon a soldier's discharge refers to his character regarded from both points of view: as a soldier and as a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character statements therefore encompass conduct in service and general moral character (C. 15359, Oct. 10, 1903).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board appointment provisions directory — noncompliance doesn't invalidate an executed discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of Army Regulations relating to appointment of a board of officers to determine facts relative to a soldier's character is directory only and does not affect the validity of an executed discharge with reference to which the directions have not been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to convene the recommended board does not necessarily void an otherwise executed discharge (C. 5943, March, 1899; 12942, July 11, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge 'for the convenience of the Government' — liberal construction and parity
rubrics_metrics.description: All soldiers honorably discharged by the Government on its own motion or for its own advantage after having served over half their enlistment and before the expiration of their term of enlistment are equally deserving; a discharge for any of these causes is 'for the convenience of the Government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes encouraging reenlistment and convenience-of-government discharges are to be liberally construed to accomplish Congressional purpose; no distinction should be made among such honorably discharged soldiers (U. 23547, Mar. 28, 1910; 28327, May 10, 1911).
